title: I have 0 coding skills (I’m a Biologist). I used AI to build a full Roguelike Deckbuilder from scratch. Here is the result
author: Victologo2
selftext:
Hi everyone. I wanted to share this project to show the real potential of AI for non-programmers like me.

**The Context:** I am a Zoology student. I understand insect biology, but I don't know C# or Unity. And I don't want to spend time learning it, because I don't have mucho time in my daily life. I had an idea for a game inspired by *Inscryption*, but grounded in real entomology.

**The Process:** I used AI (Google Antigravity, with Claude Sonnet and Gemini Flash and Gemini Pro Low/High) as my "Senior Developer".

* I acted as the **Game Designer** and **Logic Architect**.
* The AI acted as the **Programmer**.

I explained the logic with my own words, like "Improve the logic of being able to drag and drop cards (currently, you can click on a card in your hand and click on a space; I want it to also be possible to click, hold, drag, and drop cards onto spaces on the board)". The AI wrote the scripts, and we debugged the errors together (thanks to the console, F12).

**The Result: Arthropoda Bellum (v0.9)** It’s just a simple prototype:

* **Procedural Generation:** Random maps with branching paths.
* **Complex Logic:** A 3-resource economy (Energy vs Sacrifice vs Body Fragments) instead of simple mana.
* **Adaptive Enemy AI:** The CPU gets smarter and builds better decks as you win runs.
* **Save/Load Systems** and Deck Management.

**Why I'm sharing this:** To encourage others. If you have a game idea but think "I can't code," that barrier is gone. It took patience and a lot of prompting, but the game is real and playable.

You can try the demo (proof of concept) here:[https://victologo.itch.io/arthropoda-bellum](https://victologo.itch.io/arthropoda-bellum)

**PD: Also, do you have any recommendations for faster development?** I have been working on this for 3 weeks (100+ hours total) and still have some bugs. I plan to solve them in future versions, but sometimes I fix them only for them to break again due to code conflicts caused by the AI. First, everything is incredibly fast. Then... problems, bugs, new logic implemetation can be a headache...

replies.author: FridgeBaron
replies.body:
In my experience it has to do with game complexity and how isolated features are. Simpler games and systems seem to break way less often. A more exact prompt is also really helpful.

I also found that starting new chats for each feature helps a lot. Beyond that I often watch the thinking because sometimes it just goes off the rails. It does help that I know how to program and know what words to describe the way it's been doing things.

But if you can get things really compartmentalized(which is just good code) a lot less stuff should break when you change things since a lot less things specifically rely on each other.

comments.author: SplinterOfChaos
comments.body:
>I plan to solve them in future versions, but sometimes I fix them only for them to break again due to code conflicts caused by the AI.

Firstly, "code conflicts" refers to when using version control and trying to merge two versions of a code base with incompatible changes. What you're referring to is more professionally referred to as "playing wack-a-mole." I kid, there's no word for it. But please don't use terms with the wrong meaning.

Anyway, I think you should look into "regression testing" because whether your code is maintained by a robot or a human, there's no reason you should have to suffer through new bugs cropping up like that, and AI is especially bad at recognizing relevant parts of the code base. Humans don't always need testing to stay sane, but I'm pretty sure no non-trivial AI project is going to run smoothly if you don't test.

I've seen people use multi-agent setups where one agent acts as project manager, planning out features and another does code and it's definitely not as smooth as when a human plans a project, but it seems to keep things moving. 

Cursor released a blog about how they set up AI to build a browser, which would be overkill for a project like this, but it should give good insights about the current ideas about how to structure AI agents. [https://cursor.com/blog/scaling-agents](https://cursor.com/blog/scaling-agents)

comments.author: MakkoMakkerton
comments.body:
Game looks rad! As for recommendations for faster development, when you finally get a system in place and like the way it's working, be sure to "freeze" it so that it does not get affected by other changes on other features that also have interaction with the feature you are happy with. 

I have reduced the number of bugs I have run into when using AI to code different games by stressing that once something is complete, it is complete and not to be altered unless specifically told otherwise. Hope this helps and looking forward to future updates on your game!

I actually decided not to use Unity for this specific project. I am building the game using React + TypeScript, wrapped in Electron to run as a desktop app.

My reasoning was that AI agents (like Antigravity) are incredibly powerful at writing text-based code (logic, UI components, styling).   
  
PD: I would prefer Godot because it is more flexible than Unity.

PD2: I did some testing with Godot with Cursor using Claude 3.5 last summer and didn't like the workflow (hopefully that has changed now... I'll try again in the future).

comments.author: Big-Reindeer-8221
comments.body:
This is so cool. I have a question, though...  
  
Game devs usually start by creating the documentation known as the Concept Doc (or High Concept) and then create the Game Design Document (known as The Bible or GDD). This is important (mainly for collab) because it helps prevent scope/feature creep by giving you documentation to return to if your focus shifts to new things as you're developing the game.

So, did you do any documentation and if not, can you share any of your methods for organization and documentation?

replies.author: Victologo2
replies.body:
Great question! Yes, I treat documentation as a critical part of the codebase, specifically *because* I am working with AI.

Instead of a separate GDD, I keep Markdown files directly in the project root (e.g., 

GAME\_DESCRIPTION.md, [rules.md](http://rules.md), `mechanics.md`). This serves two purposes:



1. It helps me stay organized.
2. It acts as the 'Context' for the AI. Whenever I start a new task, the AI reads these files to understand the game's rules and scope, which prevents it from hallucinating features or breaking established mechanics. It effectively turns the GDD into a living part of the compiler context

replies.author: Victologo2
replies.body:
1. **CSS/DOM for UI & Cards:** The main game board and cards are actually standard HTML elements styled with advanced CSS (transforms for 3D perspective, keyframe animations, backdrop-filter for glass effects). React's virtual DOM handles the updates efficiently.
2. **PixiJS (WebGL) for VFX:** For particle effects like explosions, fire, or complex shaders that would kill performance in pure DOM, I overlay a `canvas` layer using **PixiJS**. It gives me hardware-accelerated 2D graphics right on top of the React components.

This hybrid approach (DOM for static UI + WebGL for dynamic VFX) lets me iterate super fast on the visuals just by tweaking code/CSS, which feels very natural if you're coming from a dev background

  
(This response is made by Google Antigravity, because I don't have much idea)
